item.title: CISA Adds Four Known Exploited Vulnerabilities to Catalog
item.description:
CISA has added four new vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog, based on evidence of active exploitation.

  • CVE-2025-42884 SAP NetWeaver Improper Neutralization of Special Elements in Data Query Logic Vulnerability
  • CVE-2026-76466 Cisco Expressway Series Use of Hard-coded Credentials Vulnerability
  • CVE-2026-123890 VMWare vCenter Authentication Bypass Using an Alternate Path or Channel Vulnerability
  • CVE-2026-129448 Apache Roller Deserialization of Untrusted Data Vulnerability

These types of vulnerabilities are a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and pose significant risks to the federal enterprise. 

Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk establishes vulnerability management requirements for Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies. BOD 26-04 reinforces the importance of the KEV Catalog and requires federal agencies to prioritize rapid remediation of high-risk vulnerabilities, specifically those identified by Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) listed in CISA’s KEV Catalog on publicly exposed assets that grant total control of the asset post-exploitation, while deferring action for lower-risk vulnerabilities. BOD 26-04 further establishes basic expectations for when agencies must check whether threat actors compromised the system before the patch was applied. 

While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog vulnerabilities. CISA will continue to add vulnerabilities to the catalog that meet the specified criteria. 

Aware of an exploited vulnerability not currently listed in the KEV Catalog? Submit it for potential addition through CISA’s KEV Nomination Form. Potential KEV additions must have a CVE ID, evidence of exploitation, and clear mitigation guidance.

Drones navigating cluttered spaces often encounter openings narrower than their bodies. We present a design method that jointly optimizes a quadrotor’s geometry and how its two side arms bend on contact. TeCoBots are soft, snakelike robots that can work alone and can also grab onto each other to form chains, loops, and branches, building a new body for each task. This Carnegie Mellon University Robotics Institute seminar is from Ben Burchfiel, cofounder and CTO of Walden Robotics: “Learning in Production: Building Physical AI at Walden Robotics.”

Walden Robotics is a full-stack company building both the hardware and physical AI for general-purpose manufacturing robots. item.title: It’s Time to Settle With Russia
item.description: In October, U.S. President Donald Trump sold his eleventh-hour deal to secure diesel from Russian President Vladimir Putin—pausing sanctions that his own administration had imposed—as a boon for the negotiations to end the war in Ukraine. The arrangement, he wrote on Truth Social, was intended to keep Russia at “the bargaining table.” Of course, it was always obvious to observers that the gambit had as much or more to do with bolstering the U.S. economy and stemming a massive victory for the Democrats in this month’s midterm elections, and in that, it failed.Cynics have grounds for questioning all of Trump’s moves when it comes to Russia and Ukraine. He clearly dislikes Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky and shows a marked preference for illiberal leaders, especially those willing to give him easy wins. Still, a stopped clock can be right twice a day. And concessions such as the fuel deal are exactly what might move Russia and Ukraine closer to peace, even if they are not wholly motivated by public-spiritedness.

Summary

Successful exploitation of this vulnerability could allow attackers to corrupt application memory and cause instability or a crash, potentially leading to arbitrary code execution, if a user is convinced to open a malicious file.

Vulnerabilities

CVE-2026-127280
C-More EA9 Programming Software V6.80 does not adequately validate data read from a project file before using it in heap memory operations. A crafted file causes a heap buffer overrun during file open, resulting in heap corruption and instability within the application. An attacker can exploit this vulnerability by convincing a user to open a malicious project file delivered through common distribution channels such as email, file sharing, or removable media.
Read More

1 Affected Product

AutomationDirect C-More EA9 Programming Software <=V6.80

Product Status: known_affected

Remediations

Vendor fix
Update C-More EA9 Programming Software to V6.81: https://www.automationdirect.com/support/software-downloads

Mitigation
If you cannot update to the latest software or firmware version right away, apply the following compensating controls to reduce risk until the update can be performed. These measures are temporary and do not replace the update, which remains the primary and recommended remediation. Apply these controls as appropriate based on the vulnerability, assessed risk, operational requirements, and characteristics of your environment. Implement changes under your established management-of-change process. Before implementing isolation, access-control, or network-configuration changes, evaluate potential impacts to safety, availability, and essential operational functions. • Isolate affected engineering workstations and OT systems from external and nonessential networks, including the internet and corporate IT networks, where operationally feasible. • Disable or tightly restrict vendor, contractor, and other remote access to the affected OT environment until the vulnerability can be remediated. Where remote access is operationally required, use a hardened jump host, enforce multi-factor authentication, apply least-privilege access, and limit access to authorized, time-bound sessions. • Use trusted, dedicated OT networks for device communication. Where practicable and appropriate to the assessed risk, use dedicated or physically separated infrastructure for higher-criticality systems. Where logical segmentation is used, ensure segmentation controls are appropriately configured, secured, and monitored. • Restrict both physical and logical access to affected systems to authorized personnel only. Apply least-privilege principles to administrative, engineering, maintenance, and service access. • Configure application allowlisting, where supported, so that only trusted and pre-approved applications are permitted to execute. Block unauthorized software. • Use appropriate antivirus or endpoint detection and response (EDR) tools where supported and compatible with the affected system. Configure host-based and network firewalls to permit only required communications. • Disable unnecessary services, ports, protocols, and communication pathways associated with the affected systems. Where a service or protocol cannot be disabled for operational reasons, restrict access to trusted systems and authorized users wherever possible. • Enable and regularly review available system, security, and network logs to identify suspicious or unauthorized activity. Where appropriate, monitor communications to and from affected systems for unexpected connections or changes in network behavior. • Maintain secure, tested, and preferably offline backups of PLC programs, device configurations, engineering workstation configurations, and other information necessary to restore operations. Periodically verify that backups can be successfully restored. • Verify that critical OT functions can continue operating without unnecessary dependencies on external networks, cloud services, remote-access services, corporate IT services, or other nonessential systems. • If removable media is required to transfer files into an isolated or restricted environment, use controlled and trusted media and scan it for malicious content before use. • Continuously evaluate the risks associated with operating vulnerable or outdated firmware or software. Adjust compensating controls as the threat environment, operational requirements, or available vulnerability information changes. These compensating controls are intended to reduce exposure while remediation is pending. Organizations should prioritize applying the vendor-provided update as soon as it can be safely tested and deployed within the operational environment.

item.title: CISA Adds Three Known Exploited Vulnerabilities to Catalog
item.description:
CISA has added three new vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog, based on evidence of active exploitation.

  • CVE-2026-131914 Idunno AntiCsrf Deserialization of Untrusted Data Vulnerability 

  • CVE-2026-132165 Drupal Core Remote Code Execution Vulnerability 

  • CVE-2026-132224 Optimizely Web Experimentation External Control of Critical State Data Vulnerability 

These types of vulnerabilities are a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and pose significant risks to the federal enterprise.

Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk establishes vulnerability management requirements for Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies. BOD 26-04 reinforces the importance of the KEV Catalog and requires federal agencies to prioritize rapid remediation of high-risk vulnerabilities, specifically those identified by Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) listed in CISA’s KEV Catalog on publicly exposed assets that grant total control of the asset post-exploitation, while deferring action for lower-risk vulnerabilities. BOD 26-04 further establishes basic expectations for when agencies must check whether threat actors compromised the system before the patch was applied.

While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog vulnerabilities. CISA will continue to add vulnerabilities to the catalog that meet the specified criteria.

Aware of an exploited vulnerability not currently listed in the KEV Catalog? Submit it for potential addition through CISA’s KEV Nomination Form. Potential KEV additions must have a CVE ID, evidence of exploitation, and clear mitigation guidance.

item.title: ISC Stormcast For Wednesday, November 25th, 2026 https://isc.sans.edu/podcastdetail/10194, (Wed, Nov 25th)
Cuba: WHO Director-General's remarks at press conference – 24 November 2026
item.description:
Country: Cuba
Source: World Health Organization

¡Buenos días a todos! Muchas gracias for joining us.

First, I want to thank the Government and people of Cuba for their warm welcome.

I'm especially grateful to the Minister of Public Health, Dr José Ángel Portal Miranda, and his team.

I'm also grateful to my WHO colleagues, our Assistant Director-General for Business Operations, Mr Raul Thomas;

Our Regional Emergency Director for the Americas, Dr Ciro Ugarte;

And my colleagues at the WHO-PAHO office here in Havana, led by Dr Mario Cruz.

I also appreciated the opportunity to engage with the UN Resident Coordinator, the Country Team and members of the diplomatic community here in Havana.

Cuba’s health system has a long and proud history.

It's built on primary health care. It's universal. It trains health workers for dozens of countries.

And it has a strong record of research and biotechnology.

It’s a system built over generations, and must be protected.

Yesterday I visited the William Soler Pediatric Hospital and its Cardiocenter.

I met a little girl, just one year old, waiting for open-heart surgery.

Her mother was by her side. I also met children waiting for operations, and doctors who know exactly what those children need.

What they don't always have is the medicines, supplies, spare parts and reliable electricity they need to do it.

Fuel and energy shortages, along with sanctions on buying medicines and equipment, have put serious pressure on these services.

As the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights, Volker Türk, has warned, the tightening of fuel restrictions and sanctions is directly harming Cubans, especially the most vulnerable, and endangering lives, like the children I have already told you about earlier.

He has called for these restrictions to be lifted immediately, and I echo that call.

Cuba now has a backlog of almost 100 000 surgeries, including 12 000 children. We met some of those children. They should not have to wait for the care they need.

34 000 pregnant women cannot receive the care they need.

And some important health indicators are moving in the wrong direction.

Overall mortality has increased, and life expectancy in Cuba has decreased for the first time since records began in 1950, from 78.8 years in 2020 to 74.4 years in 2025.

Infant mortality has more than doubled, from about 4 deaths per 1000 live births to 9.9 in 2025.

Maternal mortality has also increased from 37.4 per 1000 live births in 2019 to 44.1 in 2025.

Tuberculosis cases have also increased by 50% since 2019, along with outbreaks of Oropouche, dengue and chikungunya.

The impact on children makes me especially sad.

Childhood cancer survival rates have dropped from 85% to 65% following the onset of the energy blockade in January.

During my visit to the Cardiocenter, I also met its founder, Dr Herminia Palenzuela.

She's 80 years old, and she's still teaching the next generation of paediatric cardiologists.

People like her are the reason this system keeps working.

Hospitals have stayed open, and essential services keep running.

Health workers come to work every day, often after long nights without power.

They deserve more than our appreciation. They deserve our support.

We were also briefed on the many challenges facing Cuba, including its health system, and on the 176 internal reform initiatives, understanding that it’s within Cuba’s interests to address its internal challenges.

The reforms cover all sectors, including the economy, so WHO and the whole of the UN is committed to supporting these reforms as they relate to health and the other sectors.

WHO is acting. At the hospital, we delivered medicines and medical supplies mobilized through PAHO's emergency programme.

WHO has also provided 2 million US dollars in flexible funding. We agreed with the Minister to prioritize childhood vaccination, so that no child misses the protection they're entitled to.

We'll also work with the Ministry to identify which medical equipment needs repair, and to mobilize additional resources for it.

And we'll support Cuba's scientists. We'll work with the national regulatory authority and with Cuban vaccine and biotechnology institutions to speed up the WHO processes that can bring their products to more people.

But no single agency can meet these needs alone. I call on our partners to increase their technical and financial cooperation with Cuba.

The focus should be on what matters most right now: keeping services running, protecting children and mothers, and maintaining vaccination.

Health should never be a casualty of politics. Children waiting for heart surgery should not have to wait for electricity.

WHO will continue to stand with the people of Cuba and with the health workers who serve them.

Once again, my thanks to the Minister, to all health workers, and to the Government and people of Cuba for their hospitality.

Muchas gracias, and I look forward to your questions.

item.title: World: Health inequality monitoring atlas - A global mapping of country capacities, resources, policies and practices
item.description:
Country: World
Source: World Health Organization

Please refer to the attached file.

Countries face critical gaps in health inequality monitoring systems

Health inequalities exist in every country. Yet millions of people at risk of being left behind may remain invisible in national health statistics. A new World Health Organization (WHO) report reveals that despite strong commitments, countries still face significant gaps in their ability to identify, measure and monitor health inequalities. The Health inequality monitoring atlas: a global mapping of country capacities, resources, policies and practices provides the first comprehensive global picture of national health inequality monitoring systems. Drawing on self-reported data from 161 WHO Member States, it highlights examples of encouraging progress and good practices, while also pointing to areas where further investment and support are needed.

“Health inequality monitoring is an essential function that should be embedded in the health information systems of all countries,” said Dr Ahmad Reza Hosseinpoor, Health Inequality Monitoring Team Lead at WHO. “The release of this global atlas provides an important baseline snapshot of the situation in countries, and where countries can deepen efforts to strengthen the collection, analysis and use of inequality data for the advancement of health equity.”

The findings expose a disconnect between ambition and action. While 89% of participating countries reported commitments to addressing health inequalities in national health sector strategic plans, only 65% had a ministry of health unit mandated to use inequality data and evidence. Even more striking, just one in five countries had published a dedicated national health inequality report in the previous decade.

Although many countries routinely collect and report health data by age, sex and geographical location, information on economic status, education, ethnicity, disability and migration status remains far less available. This finding was evident across data sources such as health surveys, birth and death registrations, medical records and surveillance bulletins or dashboards.

The Atlas also reveals disparities between countries. High-income countries generally have better systems for collecting, analyzing and reporting inequality data than low- and middle-income countries, but every country still has room for improvement and systems strengthening. Health inequality monitoring systems require continuous development as data systems, analytical methods and health challenges evolve. Every country has opportunities to strengthen how it generates, analyses and uses evidence on health inequalities. The Atlas identifies key priorities for strengthening health inequality monitoring systems, though these will differ according to the current maturity of health information systems and available resources. They include:

  • leadership and strategic planning for the collection and use of health inequality data;
  • inclusion of inequality measures within health goals and monitoring frameworks;
  • protection and strengthening of health data infrastructure including the expanded collection of health inequality data;
  • development of more integrated data systems, including expanding the use of electronic health records and establishing means for linking data across sources, while safeguarding data privacy and confidentiality; and
  • strengthening of analytical and reporting capacity to track progress, evaluate the impact of policies and programmes, and inform action.

WHO is supporting countries through technical assistance, capacity strengthening and practical resources available through the WHO Health Inequality Monitor. Support is also being expanded through the Health Inequality Monitoring Network and regional monitoring hubs.

The Atlas establishes a crucial global baseline and a clear call to action: to close health inequalities, countries must first be able to see and measure them, then act on the evidence, so no one is deprived of the right to health.

item.title: Sudan: Drone strike kills 10-year-old pupil attending NRC-supported school in attack on family home
item.description:
Country: Sudan
Source: Norwegian Refugee Council

A 10-year-old boy, Mohammed Ali, was killed when a drone struck his family home in the city of Omdurman, Sudan on Sunday morning, 22 November, as he was getting ready to go to his school that is supported by the Norwegian Refugee Council (NRC).

Press release

Sudan Published 25. Nov 2026 - Updated 24. Nov 2026

His cousin, a baby less than a year old who lives with the family, suffered an abdominal wound that needed stitches and is now recovering.

"My son was very creative. He would bring home random things to play with, rocks and sticks. I used to call him Al Muhandes, the Engineer," said his father, Ali. "He was so smart and always cheerful, with a pleasant smile on his face."

"Women and children are a red line. They must not be harmed in any way."

Mohammed was a Grade 3 pupil at Al Assal School, a short walk from his home, where NRC supports catch-up classes for children whose education was cut short by the war. He was the eldest of three siblings.

"Everyone loved Mohammed," said his teacher, Nadia. "He was so polite and he was making good progress. All the teachers knew him and loved him."

The school was not damaged, but teachers and pupils are in mourning.

"None of us can sleep or go back to our normal lives," said Nadia. "I came to school and the classrooms were almost empty because parents are afraid to send their children. For Mohammed and for all our children, this war must stop now."

At least 2,230 civilians were killed in Sudan between January and October this year, more than 1,630 of them in drone strikes, according to the UN Human Rights Office.

"Tragically, Mohammed was one of thousands of Sudanese civilians killed in this brutal war," said Noah Taylor, NRC's Head of Operations in Sudan. "He was at home, where he should have been safe, getting ready to go to school, the other place where children should be safe. This is not the first attack to shatter that safety, and it will unlikely be the last. How many more civilian deaths will we see until the parties to this conflict are held to account for their actions?"

NRC is working with its partners to assess the psychosocial support needs of the family, pupils and teachers, and to arrange appropriate referrals. NRC remains committed to supporting the continuation of education at the school once classes resume.

item.title: World: Justice for women and girls living with HIV: end coercion, protect survivors, end impunity
item.description:
Country: World
Source: UNAIDS

GENEVA, 25 November 2026—As the 16 Days of Activism against Gender-Based Violence begin, UNAIDS is calling on governments to end violence, coercion and discrimination against women and girls living with and at risk-of HIV, ensure access to justice for survivors and hold perpetrators accountable.

For many women and girls living with and at-risk of HIV, violence does not stop at home. It follows them into schools, online, clinics, maternity wards and even into courtrooms. Violations of bodily autonomy and reproductive rights not only cause lasting harm but also undermines trust in health systems, creating barriers to accessing HIV prevention, treatment and care and support. Women and girls living with HIV have been documenting these violations for decades and demanding accountability.

"Justice must reach the places where violence happens, including our health systems," said Winnie Byanyima, Executive Director of UNAIDS. "No woman should be sterilized without her informed consent, denied the right to make decisions about her own body or be prosecuted for feeding her child. Women living with HIV deserve dignity, care and protection—not coercion, punishment or fear. Governments must end impunity and ensure justice for survivors."

Nearly one in three women worldwide have experienced physical intimate partner violence or sexual violence in their lifetime. Only 56.3% of women aged 15–49 years who are married or in a union have full decision-making power over sex, contraception and reproductive healthcare, falling to 36.8% in sub-Saharan Africa. Gender-based violence also increases vulnerability to HIV and undermine treatment outcomes. Across 30 sub-Saharan African countries, women experiencing intimate partner violence are more than three times as likely to have recently acquired HIV. Women living with HIV who experience violence are less likely to achieve viral suppression, and adolescents living with HIV who had experienced intimate partner violence and sexual abuse were half as likely to adhere to HIV treatment.

In 2026, the International Community of Women Living with HIV (ICW) released Confronting Coercion, Continued, an update to its 2024 Global Scan, analyzing data from more than 24,821 women living with HIV aged 18–49 across 48 countries. The findings revealed that 8.8% experienced some form of reproductive coercion in the preceding 12 months, including pressure to undergo sterilization, with the highest regional prevalence reported in Latin America (18.6%). Mistreatment in healthcare settings was reported by 14.5% of women accessing HIV care, rising to 23.9% among those accessing non-HIV healthcare. These experiences included denial of care, verbal and physical abuse and discriminatory treatment. Women from key populations, including sex workers and women who use drugs, younger women, and those facing economic insecurity were disproportionately affected.

“Reproductive coercion, mistreatment and abuse in healthcare settings are forms of violence that too often remain invisible and unchallenged. Documenting these violations is essential, but evidence alone is not enough. Women living with HIV must have access to justice, meaningful accountability and effective remedies when their rights are violated,” said Sophie Brion, Director of Global Programs at ICW.

Despite growing evidence about the safety of breastfeeding for women living with HIV on ART and the lifelong benefits of breastfeeding for children; women living with HIV around the world face punishments and even criminalization for decisions about how they feed their children. A 2025 ICW Latina study involving 317 women living with HIV across 19 countries in the Latin American & Caribbean Region found that 70% had never received clear or complete information about breastfeeding from health workers, while nearly one in three had been told not to breastfeed. According to HIV Justice Network, more than a dozen cases of women living with HIV are criminally prosecuted for breastfeeding or comfort nursing.

Women-led organizations and networks of women and girls living with HIV are at the forefront of documenting violations, supporting survivors, challenging discriminatory laws and practices, and demanding accountability. Their leadership is essential to protecting rights and ensuring access to HIV services. Yet this work cannot be sustained without adequate, flexible and long-term funding.

Through the 2026 Political Declaration on HIV and AIDS, Member States renewed their commitments to eliminating all forms of sexual and gender-based violence, ensuring access to justice for survivors and reducing gender inequalities and violence affecting women and girls. These commitments must now translate into concrete action.

This 16 Days of Activism, UNAIDS stands with women living with HIV, their networks and partners in calling on governments to:

  • End reproductive coercion and violence in health care, including forced or coerced sterilization, contraception and infant-feeding practices, and guarantee informed consent, bodily autonomy, confidentiality and respectful care.
  • Ensure justice and accountability for survivors, including effective remedies and reparations, and end the criminalization of women living with HIV for infant-feeding decisions.
  • Invest in women living with HIV and women-led networks through sustained, flexible funding for survivor support, advocacy, accountability and meaningful participation.

As this campaign brings us to World AIDS Day on 1 December, UNAIDS reinforces this year's message: Ending AIDS starts with access. For women and girls living with and at risk-of HIV, this means more than access to health services. It means access to rights, justice, bodily autonomy and care that is free from violence, coercion and discrimination. There can be no equal access to HIV prevention, treatment and care without the protection of women's and girls' rights. Ending violence and impunity is essential to ending AIDS.

UNAIDS

The Joint United Nations Programme on HIV/AIDS (UNAIDS) leads and inspires the world to achieve its shared vision of zero new HIV infections, zero discrimination and zero AIDS-related deaths. UNAIDS unites the efforts of 11 UN organizations—UNHCR, UNICEF, WFP, UNDP, UNFPA, UNODC, UN Women, ILO, UNESCO, WHO and the World Bank—and works closely with global and national partners towards ending the AIDS epidemic by 2030 as part of the Sustainable Development Goals. Learn more at unaids.org and connect with us on Facebook, Twitter, Instagram and YouTube.

item.title: Sudan: INGOs Call for protection of civilians and humanitarian operations following drone strikes in Nyala and Khartoum
item.description:
Country: Sudan
Source: Sudan INGO Forum

Please refer to the attached file.

Nairobi, 24 November 2026 – International non-governmental organisations working in Sudan remain alarmed by the escalating use of drones and its toll on civilians. According to the UN Human Rights Office, at least 2,230 civilians were killed between January and October 2026, more than 1,630 of them in drone strikes, and the toll is likely higher. Drone strikes also continue to damage the infrastructure civilians need to survive and to disrupt life-saving assistance.

Recent incidents in Nyala and Khartoum have again put civilians, including humanitarian personnel, in harm’s way. On 19 November, multiple strikes reportedly hit the Al Mazad district of Nyala, South Darfur, a civilian area close to humanitarian premises. On 22 November, drone strikes in Khartoum damaged a UN premises in a residential neighbourhood while personnel were inside. These incidents are not isolated. This is the Forum’s seventh alert on drone strikes this year.

Attacks directed at civilians, including humanitarian personnel, and indiscriminate attacks are prohibited under International Humanitarian Law (IHL). While the targets and circumstances of these attacks have not been independently verified, all parties must distinguish between civilian objects and military objectives. They must take all feasible precautions to protect civilians from the effects of attacks and, to the extent feasible, avoid locating military objectives within or near densely populated areas, including humanitarian premises.

Humanitarian workers, including Sudanese local and national responders, are civilians and must be respected and protected. They are present to support people affected by the conflict and humanitarian crisis. When they cannot work safely, communities risk losing access to essential assistance.

INGOs in Sudan call on all parties to the conflict to:

• Protect civilians, including humanitarian personnel. Fulfil obligations under IHL and commitments under the Jeddah Declaration; do not direct attacks against civilians and civilian objects; take all feasible precautions to avoid and minimise civilian harm; and refrain from using means and methods of warfare that cannot discriminate between military objectives and civilians.

• Keep military personnel and assets away from civilian areas and humanitarian premises, and relocate those already present wherever feasible.

• Allow full, rapid, safe, unhindered and sustained humanitarian access, including across conflict lines, so that life-saving humanitarian assistance can reach civilians in need.
